analyses.title: Performance Evaluation and Error Analysis for Multimodal Reference Resolution in a Conversation System
analyses.research_question: How well does a graph-matching multimodal reference resolver perform in real-time speech-and-gesture conversation, what causes its failures, and what design strategies can make reference resolution more robust?
analyses.methodology: The authors evaluate a deployed multimodal conversation system in a map-based real-estate domain where users communicate through speech and pointing or circling gestures. Referring expressions and candidate referents are represented as graphs containing semantic, temporal, conversational, and visual information, and reference resolution is performed by graph matching. Eleven users each performed five tasks, producing 219 evaluated inputs, and the authors conducted quantitative error analysis together with analysis of speech-gesture timing. Speech recognizers were individually trained for the participants to reduce recognition errors before the study.

key_findings.finding: The resolver correctly identified the intended referents for 137 of 219 evaluated user inputs.
Thirty-one of the 219 inputs, about 14%, were complex inputs containing multiple referring expressions that all had to be resolved correctly.
Speech-recognition errors were the largest observed error source, accounting for 55% of the reference-resolution errors.
Among 90 inputs in which referring expressions were not correctly recognized by speech recognition, multimodal information still allowed 26 references to be resolved correctly.

Gesture and speech order was not fixed: gestures preceded referring expressions in most cases, but users also produced overlapping and speech-before-gesture patterns, motivating relative temporal proximity rather than a rigid ordering rule.

The authors argue that robustness improves when temporal constraints are combined with semantic and contextual constraints and when uncertain intermediate interpretations are retained rather than discarded prematurely.

limitations: The empirical study involved only 11 users and one map-based real-estate application, limiting evidence about generalization to other interfaces and document types.
The interaction model used manual pointing and circling gestures rather than references into hierarchical document structures such as pages, regions, tables, and cells.
A two-second idle interval was used to synchronize multimodal input boundaries, and synchronization itself contributed to observed errors.

The implemented referent graph represented objects introduced through gestures, conversation history, and visual focus rather than exhaustively representing every visible object, which limited some proper-name-only references.
More than half of the participants were non-native English speakers, while speech recognition remained a major source of error despite individual recognizer training.
No public code or evaluation dataset release was reported in the paper.
raw_claims: The system resolves references by matching a graph of referring expressions against a graph of possible referents.
The referent representation incorporates information from gestures, conversational history, and visual context.
The evaluation contained 219 multimodal user inputs collected from 11 participants performing five tasks each.
The intended referents were correctly identified for 137 evaluated inputs.
About 14% of the evaluated inputs contained multiple referring expressions.
Speech-recognition failures were responsible for the largest share of observed resolution errors.
Multimodal evidence recovered some references even when their spoken referring expressions had been recognized incorrectly.
Most gestures began before their corresponding referring expressions, but this ordering was not universal.
Users could change their speech-gesture timing pattern during the same interaction.
The authors recommend combining temporal, semantic, and contextual evidence rather than treating temporal order as an absolute constraint.

analyses.title: SpreadCluster: Recovering Versioned Spreadsheets through Similarity-Based Clustering
analyses.research_question: Can spreadsheet versions whose explicit version history has been lost be recovered reliably by clustering spreadsheets according to structural and textual similarities in their worksheets and table headers?
analyses.methodology: The authors first inspect known spreadsheet evolution groups and identify table headers and worksheet names as useful version-related features. SpreadCluster extracts and cleans these features, computes worksheet similarity using textual representations of header contents together with worksheet-name information, derives spreadsheet-level similarities, and applies an adapted single-linkage clustering procedure. Similarity thresholds are learned by sweeping candidate threshold values against a manually curated training set derived from VEnron. The approach is then evaluated on Enron, EUSES, and FUSE spreadsheet corpora and compared with a filename-based version-recovery method.

key_findings.finding: On the Enron evaluation, SpreadCluster produced 1,561 candidate evolution groups, of which 1,226 were manually validated as correct, corresponding to 78.5% precision.
Against the constructed Enron ground truth of 1,609 evolution groups, SpreadCluster achieved 70.7% recall and a 74.4% F-measure.
The filename-based comparison method achieved 59.8% precision, 48.7% recall, and 53.7% F-measure on the same evaluation, substantially below the reported SpreadCluster metrics.
The learned worksheet- and spreadsheet-level similarity thresholds were 0.60 and 0.33 respectively after threshold search on the curated training data.
On EUSES the method reported 170 correct groups among 213 detected groups, or 79.8% precision, while a manually inspected sample of 200 FUSE groups produced 91.0% precision.

The recovered VEnron2 collection contains substantially more spreadsheet evolution groups and spreadsheets than the earlier VEnron collection, demonstrating that content-based recovery can expose additional version relationships missed by the earlier construction.

SpreadCluster clusters spreadsheets into evolution groups but does not automatically recover the chronological or parent-child ordering of versions; the paper states that version order was recovered manually and leaves automatic ordering for future work.

limitations: The method recovers membership in version/evolution groups rather than a directed lineage graph or automatic chronological ordering among individual spreadsheet versions.
Parallel evolution or branching versions are placed in the same evolution group rather than explicitly represented as forks in a provenance graph.
Header extraction is heuristic and can fail for spreadsheets containing primarily numerical or date-like headers, charts, data without recognizable headers, or other atypical layouts.
Worksheets with little meaningful content or generic worksheet names provide weak discriminative evidence.

The Enron ground truth was constructed using manual validation and the union of candidates found by SpreadCluster and a filename-based method, so evolution groups missed by both methods could remain absent.
Manual validation can introduce judgment errors despite cross-checking by multiple authors.
The authors identify representativeness of the evaluated spreadsheet corpora as a threat to external validity.
No public implementation of SpreadCluster was reported in the paper.
raw_claims: Spreadsheet files frequently lose explicit version information when they are copied, renamed, emailed, or moved.
Versions belonging to the same evolution group often retain similar worksheet names and table headers.
SpreadCluster uses worksheet names and table-header contents as its principal similarity features.
Formula text is not used as a principal version feature because ordinary spreadsheet evolution can change formulas even when versions remain closely related.
Spreadsheet similarity is derived from similarities among worksheets and then used by a clustering procedure.
Threshold parameters are learned from a manually curated set of known spreadsheet evolution groups.
SpreadCluster reports higher precision, recall, and F-measure than the filename-based comparison on the Enron evaluation.
The method was evaluated on spreadsheet collections from Enron, EUSES, and FUSE.
The resulting VEnron2 dataset expands the set of known evolution groups beyond the earlier VEnron dataset.
The reported method does not itself infer version ordering inside an evolution group.
Automatic recovery of version order is identified as future work.

analyses.title: Detecting and visualizing inter-worksheet smells in spreadsheets
analyses.research_question: Which inter-worksheet dependency smells occur in spreadsheets, how can they expose potential spreadsheet-quality problems, and can enriched data-flow diagrams effectively communicate those smells to spreadsheet developers?
analyses.methodology: The authors define four spreadsheet smells derived from software-engineering code-smell concepts: Inappropriate Intimacy, Feature Envy, Middle Man, and Shotgun Surgery. They compute dependency metrics over formulas that reference other worksheets and derive medium, high, and very-high risk thresholds from the 70th, 80th, and 90th percentiles of metric distributions in a large spreadsheet corpus. The smells are visualized by enriching worksheet-level data-flow diagrams with dependency information and smell indications. Evaluation combines a quantitative study over the EUSES corpus with a qualitative study involving ten professional spreadsheet developers examining industrial spreadsheets.

key_findings.finding: Feature Envy was the most prevalent of the reported inter-worksheet smells in the corpus study, with 12.4% of spreadsheets exceeding the 70th-percentile threshold.
Inappropriate Intimacy was also common, with 9.6% of spreadsheets exceeding the corresponding 70th-percentile threshold.

In the industrial study, participants distinguished benign and problematic instances of Inappropriate Intimacy, showing that a high metric value is an indicator requiring interpretation rather than direct proof of a defect.

For observed Feature Envy cases, participants agreed that refactoring could improve the spreadsheet, although understanding the exact cause often required inspecting formulas in addition to the visualization.
Shotgun Surgery instances were regarded by the participating spreadsheet developers as design shortcomings and prompted discussion of structural adaptations.
Participants generally found smell-enriched data-flow diagrams useful for understanding inter-worksheet dependencies, but some smells required lower-level formula inspection for diagnosis.

The paper explicitly notes that its dependency visualization represents the current spreadsheet structure rather than explaining why it evolved that way, and it proposes retaining spreadsheet history and changes as future work.

limitations: The analysis focuses on formula dependencies and does not model other spreadsheet mechanisms such as pivot tables, charts, or VBA code.
The smell metrics identify unusual coupling patterns but do not by themselves establish that a calculation error or user-visible defect exists.
The visualization represents worksheet dependencies in a current workbook snapshot and does not provide cross-version cell or worksheet lineage.
The authors explicitly identify spreadsheet-history storage and change documentation as future work rather than functionality evaluated in this study.
The ten-spreadsheet industrial study is small and drawn from one organizational setting.
The professional participants had taken part in an earlier evaluation of spreadsheet data-flow diagrams, which may affect responses to the visualization.
The industrial spreadsheets used in the qualitative evaluation are not reported as a public dataset.
The paper describes the implementation technology for the Breviz tool but does not report a public source-code release.
raw_claims: The paper adapts software code-smell concepts to dependencies between spreadsheet worksheets.
Four inter-worksheet smells are defined: Inappropriate Intimacy, Feature Envy, Middle Man, and Shotgun Surgery.
Risk levels are based on percentile thresholds calculated from dependency metrics over a large spreadsheet corpus.
Data-flow diagrams represent worksheets as nodes and inter-worksheet formula references as directed dependencies.
The quantitative evaluation uses spreadsheets from the EUSES corpus.
Feature Envy occurs more frequently than the other reported smells at the medium-risk threshold.
Inappropriate Intimacy is the second prominent smell reported in the corpus results.
Ten professional spreadsheet developers participated in the qualitative industrial evaluation.
Participants found the visualization useful for locating problematic dependency structures but sometimes needed to inspect formulas for detailed diagnosis.
A dependency smell is not necessarily an error because some high-coupling structures have legitimate purposes.
The evaluated tool describes a workbook's current dependency structure rather than its historical evolution.
The authors propose storing workbook history and documenting changes as a direction for future work.

analyses.title: Tracing the lineage of view data in a warehousing environment
analyses.research_question: How can the exact source data items that produced a selected item in a materialized warehouse view be formally defined and traced consistently in a multisource data-warehousing environment?
analyses.methodology: The paper takes a formal data-provenance approach rather than an empirical document-analysis approach: it defines the view-data-lineage problem for materialized warehouse views and develops lineage-tracing algorithms for relational views, including views involving aggregation. It also proposes mechanisms intended to provide consistent lineage tracing when warehouse data is derived from multiple sources. The accessible abstract describes the formal and algorithmic contributions but does not report an experimental benchmark.

key_findings.finding: The paper defines view-data lineage as identifying the source data items that produced a selected data item in a materialized warehouse view.
The authors develop lineage-tracing algorithms for relational views that include aggregation.
The work proposes mechanisms for performing consistent lineage tracing in a warehouse assembled from multiple source systems.
The proposed lineage capability is intended to support drill-through from a selected warehouse view tuple to the exact source tuples that produced it.

limitations: Only an abstract-level source could be opened, so detailed operator definitions, proofs, algorithms, and any evaluation described elsewhere in the paper could not be independently inspected.
The accessible abstract does not report an empirical dataset, runtime measurements, accuracy measurements, or other quantitative evaluation metrics.
The lineage unit is relational source and view data rather than multimodal document elements such as pages, regions, worksheets, or cells.
The accessible material does not address matching semantically corresponding elements across independently revised document versions.
No source-code or dataset release is identified in the accessible abstract.
raw_claims: The lineage problem starts with a selected data item in a materialized warehouse view.
Its objective is to identify the source data items that produced that view item.
The authors formally define this lineage problem.
They develop lineage-tracing algorithms for relational views.
The stated algorithmic scope includes aggregation.
The paper addresses consistency when lineage is traced across multiple warehouse sources.
An intended application is interactive drill-through from warehouse view tuples to their producing source tuples.

analyses.title: The T-Recs Table Recognition and Analysis System
analyses.research_question: Can table structure and page layout be recovered from word-level document segments through bottom-up spatial clustering rather than relying on explicit ruling lines or large whitespace separators?
analyses.methodology: T-Recs starts from word segments and performs bottom-up spatial clustering to construct larger layout elements instead of recursively splitting pages at detected separators. The recognized layout is then analyzed geometrically by constructing row and column structures and a regular tile representation from which table cells can be represented. The approach is designed to work without depending on textual semantics, allowing the same structural process to be applied to mixed-mode documents and OCR-derived input. The accessible author-uploaded full-text material illustrates sparse, irregular, and non-Manhattan layouts and discusses reconstruction of rows, columns, and cells, but it does not expose a modern benchmark-style quantitative evaluation.

key_findings.finding: T-Recs reverses the dominant separator-first strategy of its time by clustering word segments bottom-up into layout structures.
The subsequent table analysis constructs a tile structure representing the intersections of inferred row and column structure.
The system is designed to recognize structures containing row-spanning or column-spanning cells and sparse tables rather than requiring every table position to contain data.
The recognition procedure can operate without relying on textual content, making its layout logic language-independent in principle.
The approach is intended for mixed-mode pages and for noisy OCR-derived documents such as facsimiles rather than only clean, explicitly ruled tables.
The accessible full-text examples show that some initially clustered structures require heuristic post-processing to separate columns that have been incorrectly glued together.

limitations: The method recognizes table structure within a document snapshot but does not establish lineage between table cells or regions in different document versions.
Its input abstraction assumes that word segments and their bounding geometry have already been obtained, so upstream OCR and segmentation quality can affect later structure recovery.
Heuristic post-processing is required for cases in which initial spatial clustering incorrectly joins columns or other structures.

The accessible full-text presentation emphasizes illustrative layouts and structural behavior rather than a clearly specified large annotated benchmark with precision, recall, or comparable modern evaluation metrics.
No public source-code release was identified in the material read.
No reusable annotated evaluation dataset was identified in the material read.
raw_claims: T-Recs begins with word-level segments rather than first searching for explicit table separators.
Spatially related word segments are clustered bottom-up into larger layout blocks.
Recognized blocks are analyzed to locate table environments and recover row and column structure.
Row and column separators define a two-dimensional grid whose areas are called table tiles.
The tile representation provides a basis for representing reconstructed table structure.
The method is intended to handle empty cells and cells spanning multiple rows or columns.
Sparse tables are part of the targeted layout class.
Textual content can be ignored during structural analysis.
The authors therefore describe the method as domain- and language-independent at the structural level.
The approach is intended to tolerate low-quality OCR documents.
Some segmentation errors require targeted heuristic restructuring before the table structure is reconstructed.
